Hierarchical user requirements synthesized from 6 interview records addressing global Copilot chat history across VS Code workspaces. Four MUST requirements establish core functionality (global persistence, zero data loss, performance thresholds, coexistence strategy). Two SHOULD requirements address telemetry validation and team knowledge-sharing. MoSCoW prioritization reflects pain point severity (context loss, knowledge silos) and deployer criticality (data reliability). All requirements traced to enduser confirmations and interview resolutions per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.

Deployer dialogue targets eight critical dimensions: (1) centralized vs. distributed storage architecture for global chat history, (2) encryption and compliance constraints for user-scoped UUIDs, (3) scalability thresholds for concurrent workspace switches and session volume growth, (4) coexistence strategy and conflict resolution during JSONL-to-global migration, (5) fallback behavior and RTO/RPO SLAs if global store fails, (6) post-ship telemetry signals beyond operationalized metrics, (7) access control model for team-based chat sharing, and (8) deprecation timeline and legacy storage handling. Chain-of-thought reasoning decomposes the requirement into infrastructure, security, performance, and operational concerns aligned to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and BABOK v3 trade-off analysis.

Targeted deployer interview probing infrastructure constraints (storage backend, replication, failover), security mandates (encryption, access control, audit logging), and scalability expectations (storage growth, telemetry pipeline capacity, conflict resolution). Questions grounded in MUST requirements for <500ms latency, ≥99.5% sync rate, zero data loss, and coexistence strategy. Chain-of-Thought reasoning: (1) Decomposed user-account-scoped UUID and global chat persistence into infrastructure, security, and scalability dimensions; (2) Mapped telemetry success criteria to deployer observability capabilities; (3) Surfaced migration risks (fallback logic, conflict resolution) to validate deployment readiness.

Targeted questions probe deployment architecture (centralized vs. distributed storage), security mandates (auth, encryption, data isolation for team collaboration), scalability thresholds (user concurrency, growth trajectory, fallback impact), migration risk (JSONL deprecation timeline, legacy version support, rollback), telemetry operationalization (SLA validation gates, data retention, confirmation mechanism), and disaster recovery (RTO/RPO, failover). Chain-of-Thought reasoning decomposed requirements into infrastructure, security, performance, operational, and reliability dimensions aligned with ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 stakeholder validation and MoSCoW prioritization.

Deployer constraints mandate distributed persistence with <500ms retrieval latency, encryption-at-rest/transit, 99.5% sync completion, zero data loss via WAL + fallback, dual-write coexistence strategy, telemetry-driven SLA validation at ship-time, and tiered cost optimization. Migration requires 2+ release deprecation window with automated rollback triggers.

Deployer response operationalizes global chat history across VS Code workspaces via distributed cloud persistence (Settings Sync backend) with user-account-scoped UUID indexing, <500ms retrieval latency, and ≥99.5% sync completion. Security enforced through TLS 1.3+, AES-256 encryption, and audit logging; coexistence with per-workspace JSONL fallback ensures zero data loss during transition. Scalability targets 10M+ concurrent users; operational procedures establish canary rollout with telemetry validation before full adoption; cost optimized via tiered caching and existing infrastructure reuse.

Deployer constraints mandate distributed cloud persistence with <500ms UUID-indexed retrieval, AES-256 encryption at-rest and TLS 1.3+ in-transit, role-based access controls, and secure JSONL fallback coexistence. Scalability targets require 10K concurrent workspace-switch events/sec with tiered storage. Operational procedures enforce pre-deployment telemetry validation (latency, 99.5% sync rate, zero data loss) and gradual rollout with feature flags. Cost optimization leverages existing Settings Sync infrastructure with client-side deduplication. Availability design includes 99.95% SLA, multi-region replication, and graceful degradation to per-workspace JSONL during outages.

Deployer role identifies six critical operational clarifications blocking infrastructure implementation: (1) distributed persistence layer selection and cost-performance trade-offs, (2) encryption key management during profile migrations, (3) fallback activation criteria and reconciliation logic, (4) secure purge procedures for legacy JSONL files, (5) audit logging scope and retention, (6) scalability validation under expected load. These questions address infrastructure constraints, security mandates, and availability-cost-performance trade-offs required to operationalize global chat history deployment per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standards.

Deployer role requires clarification on seven critical operational gaps: (1) designated persistence layer and SLA guarantees, (2) encryption key management strategy and rotation policy, (3) explicit fallback activation thresholds and escalation sequence, (4) read-replica cache architecture and invalidation logic, (5) secure purge procedures for JSONL deprecation, (6) infrastructure scaling capacity and cost trade-offs, and (7) audit logging scope and retention. These clarifications are essential to operationalize the global chat history requirements (UUID-scoped persistence, <500ms retrieval latency, ≥99.5% sync rate, zero data loss) within ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 deployment constraints.
